This page is the part the diagrams skip: how to create QEMU nodes that boot reliably, how to address every link so two nodes agree on a subnet, how to add static and OSPF routes, how to get out to the internet without leaking lab traffic, and how to prove the path with counters instead of hope. KVM accelerated static + OSPF link capture 4-node topology 01 Emulation, not simulation Packet Tracer simulates; GNS3 runs real operating systems and real routing daemons. That means real kernel behaviour, real bugs, and real resource cost. Choose the node type by what you are testing. Node type What runs Use it for Cost QEMU VM A full OS image on KVM Linux routers, firewalls, appliances, anything with a kernel RAM and CPU per node Docker A container on the GNS3 host Quick Linux endpoints and services Shares the host kernel Ethernet switch Virtual switch with ports Layer-2 labs, VLAN tagging Nearly free Cloud / NAT node A bridge to the host Reaching the LAN or the internet Easy to misconfigure The rules of a routed lab are boring and absolute: every link is its own subnet, every node knows the subnet of its own interfaces, and every node has a route for everything it cannot reach directly. When that is true, ping works; when it is not, no amount of GNS3 icons will help. 02 Install the server and the GUI Two shapes: the GNS3 VM (a packaged server, required for QEMU on Windows and macOS) or a headless gns3-server on Linux, with the GUI talking to it over HTTP. The headless shape is easier to back up and to keep off the internet. sudo apt update sudo apt install -y gns3-server gns3-gui qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils \\ libvirt-daemon-system ovs-vswitchd gns3server --version systemctl --user status gns3-server 2>/dev/null | head -5 ss -ltnp | grep 3080 # the API port; keep it on 127.0.0.1 # KVM present, and usable by your user kvm-ok 2>/dev/null || egrep -c "(vmx|svm)" /proc/cpuinfo ls -l /dev/kvm No KVM, no lab Without /dev/kvm access, QEMU falls back to software emulation and a four-node lab crawls. Add your user to the kvm group, or run the GNS3 server as the user who owns the images — and never on a host where you also run production VMs you care about. Bind the server to 127.0.0.1 in the server config unless you are deliberately running it headless on another machine, and keep that machine on a management network, not on the internet. 03 Design before you click Write the addressing plan first. It is the only part of the lab that cannot be fixed by clicking harder, and it is what makes a route table readable. Segment Subnet Nodes Purpose transit-a 10.10.1.0/30 r1 .1, r2 .2 Point-to-point link, only two usable addresses transit-b 10.10.2.0/30 r2 .1, r3 .2 Second hop of the path lan-1 10.10.11.0/24 r1 .1, host .10 Where the client lives lan-3 10.10.13.0/24 r3 .1, host .10 Destination segment mgmt GNS3 internal Server only The GUI and console traffic, never routed into the lab Four nodes are enough to learn everything on this page: r1 and r2 and r3 as routers, plus one host. Draw it on paper, then reproduce it. The diagram is documentation, not decoration. 04 QEMU nodes: disk, console, adapters Create the image once, boot it outside GNS3 to install the OS, then register it as a template. Booting inside GNS3 first is how people lose an afternoon to a black console. # one disk per node role, thin-provisioned qemu-img create -f qcow2 r1.qcow2 8G # install the OS outside GNS3: serial console, one virtio NIC qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -m 512 -smp 2 \ -drive file=r1.qcow2,if=virtio \ -netdev user,id=n0 -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=n0 \ -nographic Template field Value Why Binary qemu-system-x86_64 Match the architecture of the image RAM / CPUs 512 MB, 2 vCPU for a router Four routers must fit in the host's budget Adapters virtio-net-pci , count set explicitly The count must equal the links you will draw Console Telnet with -nographic , or VNC Telnet needs a serial console configured in the guest Options -enable-kvm -smp 2 Without KVM the lab is unusable Disk Per-node qcow2 copy Nodes must not share a writable disk Serial console, or you cannot log in Add console=ttyS0 to the kernel command line (and enable a getty on it) before you register the template. GNS3's telnet console is a serial line: without a getty, you get a blank screen and assume the node failed. 05 Addressing and the first route GNS3 connects cables; it does not assign addresses. Configure each interface inside the guest, with the subnet from your plan, then verify before adding more. # inside r1 sudo ip addr add 10.10.1.1/30 dev ens3 sudo ip addr add 10.10.11.1/24 dev ens4 sudo ip link set ens3 up && sudo ip link set ens4 up sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 # make it survive a reboot echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-lab.conf ip -br addr ip route ping -c2 10.10.11.10 # the host on the LAN segment Two details catch almost everyone: the /30 on a point-to-point link (so the two ends agree on scope), and the interface names, which depend on how many virtio adapters the template created. Match ens3 / ens4 to what the guest actually reports. 06 Static routing across three segments With three routers, static routes make the forwarding logic visible: each router only needs to know its directly connected subnets and a next hop for the rest. # r1: everything on the far side goes to r2 sudo ip route add 10.10.2.0/30 via 10.10.1.2 sudo ip route add 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.1.2 # r2: both LANs are behind neighbours sudo ip route add 10.10.11.0/24 via 10.10.1.1 sudo ip route add 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.2.2 # r3: mirror image of r1 sudo ip route add 10.10.1.0/30 via 10.10.2.1 sudo ip route add 10.10.11.0/24 via 10.10.2.1 # prove it, hop by hop ip route get 10.10.13.10 traceroute -n 10.10.13.10 ping -c2 10.10.13.10 A missing route shows up as "Destination Net Unreachable" or a silent timeout. Read ip route get on each hop before blaming GNS3: the emulator is almost never the problem when one subnet is unreachable. 07 Dynamic routing with FRR Once the static version works, replace the routes with a routing protocol and watch the tables build themselves. FRR installs from the distro and runs the same daemons as a real router. sudo apt install -y frr # enable the daemon before it will run sudo sed -i 's/^ospfd=no/ospfd=yes/' /etc/frr/daemons sudo systemctl restart frr sudo vtysh -c 'configure terminal' \ -c 'router ospf' \ -c 'network 10.10.0.0/16 area 0' \ -c 'exit' -c 'interface ens3' -c 'ip ospf area 0' \ -c 'exit' -c 'write memory' sudo vtysh -c 'show ip ospf neighbor' sudo vtysh -c 'show ip route ospf' Same area on every router for the first lab; multi-area is a second exercise. Announce only lab subnets. A stray default route can pull your management traffic into the emulator. Check adjacency before routes: no neighbour means no LSA exchange, and no routes to debug. If you only need to test reachability, static routes are more honest: you can see every decision. Use OSPF when convergence itself is the subject. 08 Testing routes the CCNA way The CCNA asks you to read a routing table and predict the path before you touch a cable. In the lab you can check that prediction in seconds — and explain why a /24 beat a /16 that was also in the table. # r2's whole world, on one screen ip route show # 10.10.1.0/30 dev ens3 proto kernel scope link src 10.10.1.2 # 10.10.11.0/24 via 10.10.1.1 dev ens3 # 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.2.2 dev ens4 # the decision for one destination, with the winning prefix ip route get 10.10.13.10 # 10.10.13.10 via 10.10.2.2 dev ens4 src 10.10.2.1 # the same question through FRR, with its own codes sudo vtysh -c 'show ip route 10.10.13.10' Candidate in r2's table Matches 10.10.13.10? Result 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.10.1.2 Yes, length 0 Loses to every more specific route 10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2 Yes, length 16 Loses to the /24 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.2.2 Yes, length 24 Wins: longest prefix match Longest match is decided by prefix length, not by the order routes were added and not by metric. Change the /24 to a /26 and watch a different rule take over. # two equal-cost paths, one prefix sudo ip route replace 10.10.13.0/24 \ nexthop via 10.10.2.2 dev ens4 nexthop via 10.10.1.2 dev ens3 ip route show 10.10.13.0/24 # both next hops are used; counters must move on both links # prove the loop, do not guess it ping -c1 -t 2 10.10.13.10 # From 10.10.2.1 icmp_seq=1 Time to live exceeded in transit traceroute -n -m 6 10.10.13.10 # drops and errors, per interface ip -s link show ens4 Test Command Pass Otherwise Reachability ping -c2 target Replies, 0% loss Route missing, ARP failing, or a firewall in the path Path traceroute -n target Hops in the planned order Asymmetric or looping path Decision ip route get target Expected next hop and source address Shadowed route or wrong prefix Longest match Add /16 and /24 for the same target /24 wins Table order or metric being blamed for prefix length ECMP Two next hops, then traffic Counters rise on both links One link dead, or hashing pinned to one path TTL ping -t 2 , increasing TTL exceeded names the loop's router Silent drop with no ICMP at all A ping proves the forward path, not the design Return traffic can take a different route and still succeed; the lab is only understood when both directions are captured. On FRR, compare show ip route (C/S/O codes and administrative distance: static 1, OSPF 110) with the kernel table ip route — they should agree, and when they do not, zebra is not installed the route you think it is. OSPF state Meaning in this lab Down No hello received; interface not in the area, or the link is down Init Hello seen, but this router is not in the neighbour's hello 2-Way Bidirectional on a broadcast segment; normal for non-DR/BDR ExStart / Exchange Leader election and database description exchange Loading LSAs requested; a stuck Loading is a database you need to read Full Databases synchronised — now routes can appear in show ip route ospf The prefix arithmetic and administrative-distance reasoning are worked through in the CCNA/CCNP manual ; the protocol-by-protocol background is in Networking . Run each test here until the answer is obvious before you read it. 09 Internet access without leaking A lab that needs package updates needs a path out, and a lab that needs to stay contained needs that path to be one-way and explicit. Put the NAT where you can see it — on the router that faces the host. # on the edge node, whose ens3 faces the GNS3 NAT/cloud node sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o ens3 -j MASQUERADE sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i ens4 -o ens3 -s 10.10.11.0/24 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i ens3 -o ens4 -d 10.10.11.0/24 \ -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -P FORWARD DROP # verify from a LAN host ip route curl -sI https://deb.debian.org | head -1 Containment is part of the topology Forward policy DROP and a stateful allow rule are what keep the lab from becoming a router for your house. If the lab is for attack practice, isolate it completely and use a local package mirror — the defenders page explains why stray lab traffic is a detection story you do not want. 10 VLANs and switching A routed lab eventually needs a switch between routers, and a switched lab eventually needs VLANs. GNS3 ships an Ethernet switch node; verify its tagging options in your version, and use an Open vSwitch node when you need exact control. # inside an OVS node: two access ports and one trunk ovs-vsctl add-br br0 ovs-vsctl add-port br0 eth1 tag=10 ovs-vsctl add-port br0 eth2 tag=20 ovs-vsctl add-port br0 eth3 trunk=10,20 ovs-vsctl show Then address the VLANs on the router with sub-interfaces, and remember that the switch does not route: ip link add link ens4 name ens4.10 type vlan id 10 is what puts an address on a tag. 11 Capture and prove the path Right-click a link and start a capture: GNS3 shells out to dumpcap and shows the file in Wireshark. For anything scripted, take the pcap and read it yourself — the same discipline as the tcpdump manual. tshark -r link-r1-r2.pcapng -Y "icmp || ospf" -T fields \ -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e icmp.type -e ospf.msg | head -20 # the two counters that prove forwarding worked cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward nstat -az | grep -E "IpInReceives|IpOutRequests|IpInAddrErrors" Symptom on the wire What it means ICMP echo request arrives, no reply Return route missing on the far node OSPF hello one-way One interface not in the area, or MTU mismatch Repeated ARP for the gateway Wrong subnet mask, or gateway address typo Forty-byte window, no data MTU black hole; test with ping -M do -s 1400 Traffic only in one direction Only one link is captured — check the SPAN or the second cable For turning those captures into alerts, the Suricata build reads the same files offline; for the protocol background, the networking manual. 12 The paranoid checklist Check Pass condition KVM active /dev/kvm accessible; guest boot under ten seconds One subnet per link Addressing plan written; no overlap with the GNS3 management net Adapter count matches links No "interface not found" after adding a cable Forwarding on ip_forward=1 persisted in /etc/sysctl.d Routes readable ip route on each node shows only what you planned Return path tested traceroute works in both directions Forward policy explicit DROP default, stateful allow rules, no open MASQUERADE Capture kept Pcap plus the command that produced it, stored with the project Disk per node No two nodes share a writable qcow2 Project exported One archive you can rebuild from after a laptop dies 13 Common failures Symptom Cause Fix Node boots to a black console No getty on ttyS0 , or console type mismatch Add console=ttyS0 , enable the serial getty, reboot QEMU exits immediately Image path moved, or no KVM permission Check the template's disk path and ls -l /dev/kvm Only two NICs appear Template adapter count too low Edit the template, raise the count, restart the node Ping fails one way Missing return route or wrong netmask ip route get on both ends OSPF neighbour stuck in EXSTART MTU mismatch between neighbours Align MTU on both interfaces, or fix the virtual link MTU Everything is slow Software emulation, or too many vCPUs per node Enable KVM, reduce vCPU count, close the extra nodes LAN host has no internet NAT rule missing, forwarding off, or DNS absent Recheck MASQUERADE, ip_forward , and the resolver Lab traffic on the home network Cloud node bridged without a firewall Remove the bridge, use NAT with a DROP forward policy 14 Sources GNS3 — the official documentation, including QEMU templates and server setup. AV Dr. Alistair Vance & The Symbiotic Initiative Published October 2026 • Global Epistemology & Technology Review 00 Introduction: The Threshold of Co-Evolution Every major technological revolution in human history has forced a profound renegotiation of what it means to be human. The mastery of fire externalized survival; the printing press democratized cognition; the industrial engine augmented muscle. Today, artificial intelligence stands as the final frontier of tool-making: the externalization and scaling of cognition itself. Yet, public discourse remains gripped by a polarized paralysis—split violently between techno-utopians predicting an imminent paradise of automated leisure and catastrophists invoking deterministic dystopias of existential subjugation. Neither narrative captures reality. Artificial intelligence is neither a benevolent deity nor a rogue demonic entity; it is an algorithmic mirror forged from the cumulative history, data, biases, and brilliance of human civilization. It accelerates whatever dynamics we feed into it. Consequently, asking what AI will do to us is the wrong inquiry. The more urgent, uncomfortable question is: What must humanity fix within itself so that AI can elevate our species rather than automate our decay? 01 Part I: The Mirror of Intelligence When pruned of marketing hype, artificial intelligence offers unprecedented tools for civilizational uplift. By operating at combinatorial speeds impossible for biological neural networks, advanced models function across multiple transformative dimensions: 🧬 Cognitive & Scientific Synthesis Simulating complex biological pathways, protein folding, and material science discoveries in months instead of centuries, effectively compressing medical research timelines. ⚖️ Overcoming Psychological Biases Acting as an objective cognitive partner that challenges confirmation bias, analyzes systemic blind spots, and parses vast datasets free from emotional fatigue. 🕊️ Liberating Human Potential Automating bureaucratic drudgery and mechanical labor to redirect human bandwidth toward interpersonal empathy, philosophical inquiry, and creative expression. By absorbing the collective digital output of humanity, AI becomes an unsparing mirror. It reflects our cultural masterpieces alongside our historical prejudices, forcing us into a vital ontological awakening: to build a wise machine, we must confront the unresolved fractures in our own collective psyche. 02 Part II: The Reality Check Honesty demands that we confront the profound hazards and systemic frictions inherent in current AI trajectories. To romanticize artificial intelligence without acknowledging its structural pathologies is to invite catastrophe. Epistemic Drift and Hallucinations Unlike deterministic calculators, generative models synthesize probabilistic tokens based on patterns. When they invent false citations, logical fallacies, or authoritative falsehoods ("hallucinations"), they exploit human susceptibility to fluent authority—threatening to poison our epistemic commons with synthetic noise. Ecological and Energy Tolls Training and operating frontier foundation models requires staggering amounts of electrical power, specialized semiconductors, and fresh water for data center cooling. In an era of escalating climate crisis, unbridled compute scaling risks compounding ecological degradation unless decoupled from fossil fuels. The Concentration of Power and Moral Outsourcing AI development remains dangerously concentrated within a handful of monopolistic tech conglomerates backed by venture capital. Furthermore, humans increasingly suffer from moral outsourcing —delegating high-stakes judicial, medical, and ethical decisions to opaque algorithms to evade personal responsibility. The Danger of Opaque Agency "When we treat algorithms as infallible oracles rather than statistical instruments, we abdicate our moral duty and risk locking historical biases into immutable digital stone." 03 Part III: What Humans Must Improve to Elevate AI If artificial intelligence is to become a true catalyst for human flourishing rather than an amplifier of our worst impulses, humanity must undergo rigorous internal evolution. The engineering bottleneck is no longer solely in silicon; it is in human wisdom. 1. Epistemic Hygiene & Curation Shifting from gathering gargantuan unvetted datasets to curating high-integrity, ethically rigorous, and diverse knowledge corpora that prioritize truth over engagement metrics. 2. Rewriting Incentives Transitioning from attention-economy algorithms that monetize outrage and division toward alignment metrics that reward societal cohesion, scientific truth, and long-term sustainability. 3. Educational Reformation Upgrading global education away from rote memorization toward meta-cognition, rigorous skepticism, philosophical literacy, and emotional intelligence in an AI-saturated world. 4. Polycentric Governance Forging binding international treaties, transparent auditing frameworks, and inclusive global regulatory bodies that prevent unchecked corporate and nationalist arms races. Without cultivating deep emotional and philosophical maturity in our leaders, creators, and citizens, no amount of technical alignment mathematics will save us from our own short-sightedness. 04 Conclusion: The Mutual Ascent The symbiotic horizon is neither an inevitable utopia nor a guaranteed apocalypse; it is an ongoing, high-stakes negotiation between human consciousness and machine capability. As we refine our ethical frameworks, institutional resilience, and epistemic discipline, our tools will reflect that heightened wisdom back to us. The Reciprocal Evolution "We do not build AI to replace our humanity. We build AI to reveal what our humanity is truly capable of achieving when unburdened by unnecessary suffering and elevated by relentless truth." Conscious stewardship is our collective mandate. By stepping up to mend our own systemic flaws, we ensure that the dawn of artificial intelligence marks not the twilight of humanity, but the beginning of our greatest evolutionary leap.

A hands-on learning adventure · beginner to builder JavaScript From Zero to Hero A deep, friendly guide to thinking in code, making websites interactive, and understanding how JavaScript can also work outside the browser. No experience needed—just curiosity. 19 bite-sized lessons Examples from first steps to advanced No libraries needed Made for ages 12+ Your mission: Don’t memorize every word. Read a little, type the examples yourself, change them, break them, and fix them. That is how programmers learn. Ask a trusted adult before installing software or running code from strangers. 01 Think like a coder Programming is giving a computer clear instructions to solve a problem. A computer is very fast, but it does exactly what its instructions say—not what you meant. Coding is the art of turning a big idea into tiny, unambiguous steps. 🧩 1. Understand What should happen? What information do you have? What result do you want? 🪜 2. Break it down Split the job into smaller steps. A recipe is an algorithm: a list of steps in order. 🛠️ 3. Write and test Tell JavaScript the steps. Try normal, tiny, huge, and surprising inputs. 🔎 4. Improve Read what happened, fix one thing at a time, and make the code easier to understand. Algorithm before code: packing a school bag Look at tomorrow’s timetable. For each class, add its books and supplies. If it is sports day, add sports clothes. Check the list, then close the bag. Notice the words for each and if ? They become loops and decisions in code. Before typing, explain your solution in ordinary words or draw a flowchart. Vocabulary: An algorithm is a repeatable set of steps. A bug is a problem in a program. Debugging means finding and fixing that problem. Bugs are normal—even experts make them. 02 Your first JavaScript JavaScript (often shortened to JS) is a programming language that makes things happen. Try the browser console: in most desktop browsers, open Developer Tools and choose Console . Type a line and press Enter. On a phone or tablet, use an online coding environment with a trusted adult. The console is a scratchpad; it is not the same as a text message box. console.log("Hello, world!"); console.log(2 + 3); console.log() prints a value so you can inspect it. Text goes inside quotes; numbers do not. The semicolon marks the end of a statement. JavaScript often allows you to leave it out, but using it consistently can make code easier to scan. JavaScript is not Java Despite their similar names, Java and JavaScript are different languages, like a car and a carpet are different even though both start with “car”. This guide teaches JavaScript. Try it: Change the greeting to your name. Then print the answer to 12 * 4 . Predict the result before pressing Enter. 03 Values and variables Values are the information your program works with. Variables give useful names to information. Three useful ways to create a variable const learner = "Mina"; // This name should keep pointing to this value let score = 0; // This value can be updated score = score + 10; console.log(learner, score); Kind Use it when… Example const You won’t assign a different value to this variable. const homePlanet = "Earth"; let You need to assign a new value later. let lives = 3; lives = 2; var Mostly in older code; learn to recognize it, but usually prefer const or let . var oldStyle = true; A variable is like a labeled box, but const means the label cannot be pointed at a different value. If a const contains an object or array, the contents may still be changed; we will see why in Lesson 09. Common value types const username = "Kai"; // string: text const age = 12; // number: includes whole and decimal numbers const isReady = true; // boolean: true or false const score = null; // intentionally no value let nextMove; // undefined: no value assigned yet const huge = 12345678901234567890n; // bigint: very large whole number JavaScript also has symbol , used for special unique identifiers. You usually won’t need it at first. Check a value’s type with typeof —but be aware of one old JavaScript surprise: typeof null says "object" . console.log(typeof "hello"); // "string" console.log(typeof 42); // "number" console.log(typeof true); // "boolean" Text and templates const hero = "Nova"; const level = 4; const message = `${hero} reached level ${level}!`; console.log(message); Backticks create a template literal . The ${...} parts insert JavaScript values into the text. Changing values and naming let coins = 5; coins = coins + 2; // now 7 coins += 3; // now 10 coins++; // now 11 Use names that explain what a value means: minutesLeft is clearer than x . JavaScript names are case-sensitive: score and Score are different. 04 Math and comparisons Computers are great at arithmetic, counting, and checking rules. Operator Meaning Example result + Add, or join strings 7 + 2 → 9 - Subtract 7 - 2 → 5 * Multiply 7 * 2 → 14 / Divide 7 / 2 → 3.5 % Remainder after division 7 % 2 → 1 ** Power 3 ** 2 → 9 Order matters: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. Use parentheses to make your meaning obvious: (2 + 3) * 4 . Equality and comparisons console.log(5 > 3); // true console.log(5 === 5); // true: same value and type console.log(5 === "5"); // false: number is not text console.log(5 !== 4); // true: not equal Prefer === and !== for equality. The older == can convert types in surprising ways, so beginners should avoid it until they understand coercion. Comparisons include < , > , <= , >= . Logic: combine yes/no answers const hasTicket = true; const isOldEnough = true; console.log(hasTicket && isOldEnough); // AND: both must be true console.log(hasTicket || isOldEnough); // OR: either can be true console.log(!hasTicket); // NOT: flips true/false Think of logic like rules for a game. && means “and”, || means “or”, and ! means “not”. JavaScript’s && and || can return one of their original values, not just true or false ; that shortcut is useful later. Averages and rounding const points = [8, 10, 6]; const total = points[0] + points[1] + points[2]; const average = total / points.length; console.log(Math.round(average)); // 8 Computers use floating-point numbers, so some decimal calculations are tiny bit inexact (for example, 0.1 + 0.2 ). For money, store cents as whole numbers where possible: 199 cents is $1.99. 05 Make decisions Programs choose different actions with conditions. const temperature = 18; if (temperature >= 25) { console.log("Warm day!"); } else if (temperature >= 15) { console.log("A light jacket might help."); } else { console.log("Bundle up!"); } JavaScript checks conditions from top to bottom and runs the first matching branch. Curly braces { } hold the instructions in a block. Indentation is not required by the computer, but it helps people see the structure. Switch for a list of exact choices const day = "Saturday"; switch (day) { case "Saturday": case "Sunday": console.log("Weekend!"); break; default: console.log("School day"); } break stops the switch from continuing into the next case. For many simple choices, if / else is easier to read. Truthy and falsy (a later-level idea) Conditions can use values other than booleans. Values such as 0 , "" , null , undefined , and NaN act like false in a condition; most other values act like true. When learning, explicit checks can be clearer. const nickname = ""; if (nickname) { console.log(`Hi, ${nickname}!`); } else { console.log("No nickname yet."); } 06 Repeat with loops Loops save you from writing the same instruction over and over. Count with a for loop for (let round = 1; round Read it as: start at 1; keep going while the condition is true; add 1 after each turn. The three parts are separated by semicolons. Watch the condition carefully: a mistake can cause an endless loop. Repeat while something is true let energy = 3; while (energy > 0) { console.log("Play!"); energy--; } A while loop checks before each turn. Make sure each turn can eventually make its condition false. Otherwise it may never stop. Loop through a collection const snacks = ["apple", "toast", "yogurt"]; for (const snack of snacks) { console.log(`Pack: ${snack}`); } for...of is a friendly way to visit each item in an array or other iterable. Use break to stop early or continue to skip to the next turn. Loop safety: If a page freezes, a loop might be running forever. Stop the page or close its tab. In your own code, double-check the starting value, stopping condition, and update. 07 Functions: reusable recipes A function groups instructions under a name. Give it inputs; it can return an output. function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } const greeting = greet("Sam"); console.log(greeting); name is a parameter —a named input. "Sam" is an argument —the actual value we pass in. return sends a result back. A function can also do a task without returning a useful value. Function expressions and arrow functions const double = function (number) { return number * 2; }; const triple = (number) => { return number * 3; }; const quadruple = number => number * 4; console.log(double(5), triple(5), quadruple(5)); Arrow functions are a shorter way to write many functions. If the arrow function has one expression, parentheses and braces can be shortened; that expression is returned automatically. Use braces plus return when the steps need more room. Default inputs and input checking function welcome(name = "friend") { return `Welcome, ${name}!`; } function add(a, b) { if (typeof a !== "number" || typeof b !== "number") { return "Please give me two numbers."; } return a + b; } console.log(welcome()); console.log(add(4, 6)); Keep each function focused: one clear job, a helpful name, and predictable inputs and outputs. This makes it easier to test and reuse. 08 Arrays: lists of things Use an array when you have an ordered list of values. const colors = ["teal", "gold", "violet"]; console.log(colors[0]); // "teal"; the first position is 0 console.log(colors.length); // 3 colors.push("coral"); // add to the end colors.pop(); // remove the last item Array positions are called indexes and start at zero. The last valid index is array.length - 1 . A const array can still have items added or removed: the variable still points at the same array. Useful array tools const numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]; const doubled = numbers.map(number => number * 2); const bigOnes = numbers.filter(number => number >= 6); const found = numbers.find(number => number === 4); const total = numbers.reduce((sum, number) => sum + number, 0); console.log(doubled, bigOnes, found, total); Tool What it does Changes original? map Make a new array by changing each item No filter Make a new array with items that pass a test No find Get the first item that passes a test No reduce Combine items into one answer, such as a total No sort Reorder items (by default, as text) Yes For numbers, sort with a comparison rule: numbers.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b) . slice() makes a copy first, so the original list stays in its old order. Arrays of arrays const seats = [ ["A1", "A2"], ["B1", "B2"] ]; console.log(seats[1][0]); // "B1" 09 Objects: describe a thing An object groups named pieces of information, called properties. const pet = { name: "Pixel", kind: "cat", age: 3, isHungry: false }; console.log(pet.name); // dot notation console.log(pet["kind"]); // bracket notation pet.isHungry = true; Objects are useful when values belong together. A property’s name is its key . Use dot notation when you know the key; use brackets when you have the key in a variable or the name has special characters. Methods: functions that belong to objects const player = { name: "Rin", score: 0, earn(points) { this.score += points; return `${this.name} now has ${this.score} points.`; } }; console.log(player.earn(10)); In this method, this refers to the object that called it. this behaves differently in some kinds of functions; when that feels confusing, use a named parameter or read about arrow-function this rules later. Destructuring and spread const { name, score } = player; // take properties into variables const upgradedPlayer = { ...player, level: 2 }; // copy + add const newColors = [...["blue", "green"], "gold"]; // copy + add Objects are shared by reference: Assigning const otherPet = pet does not make a separate pet. Both names point to the same object. Spreading with { ...pet } makes a shallow copy: nested objects still need more care. JSON: a text format for data const saved = JSON.stringify(pet); // object → JSON text const restored = JSON.parse(saved); // JSON text → object JSON looks similar to JavaScript objects but is stricter: keys and text must use double quotes, and JSON cannot contain functions or undefined . Only parse JSON you trust or handle parse errors. 10 Scope, errors, and debugging Scope is where a name can be used. Debugging is careful detective work. const outside = "I can be used below"; function showMessage() { const inside = "I only exist in this function"; console.log(outside, inside); } showMessage(); // console.log(inside); // Error: inside is out of scope let and const are block-scoped: they live inside the nearest pair of braces where they were declared. Prefer small scopes and avoid reusing the same name for different ideas. Three kinds of problems Syntax error: the code is not written in a way JavaScript understands (perhaps a missing quote or bracket). Runtime error: the code starts, but something goes wrong while it runs. Logic bug: it runs, but gives the wrong answer. A calm debugging checklist Read the whole error message and note the line number. Check spelling, quote marks, brackets, and capitalization. Print intermediate values with console.log() . Test the smallest example that shows the problem. Change one thing, run again, and see whether it helped. Ask: what did I expect, what happened, and what is the first place they differ? function average(a, b) { const total = a + b; console.log("Checking total:", total); // temporary detective clue return total / 2; } console.log(average(8, 10)); Browser Developer Tools offer a debugger. A breakpoint pauses the program on a chosen line so you can inspect variables one step at a time. 11 JavaScript on the web: the DOM HTML describes a page, CSS styles it, and JavaScript can respond and update it. HTML The page structure: headings, buttons, paragraphs, images. CSS The appearance: colors, layout, spacing, motion. JavaScript The behavior: reacting, calculating, updating, communicating. Military: Manual Técnico · Nível de Operações Infiltrar sem ser a força: leitura de estruturas grupais e de redes criminosas Uma orientação técnica para forças de segurança que pretendem agir com precisão, justiça e sem reproduzir os erros alheios ao próprio Estado. Ref. MT-2026-04 Idioma: pt-PT Acesso por nível (sequencial) Este manual foi concebido para leitores das forças armadas, polícias e serviços de inteligência. Não ensina a cometer crimes; ensina a não cometer crimes enquanto se protege a ordem . A leitura é sequencial: cada nível depende do anterior. Nível 1 Tráfico de confusão: polícia, militar, crimes e inocência Antes de agir, é preciso saber o que é e onde . Este nível diferencia tipos de organização, distingue o inocente do criminoso e explica porque razão a “solução militar” raramente é a resposta correta. 1.1 Tipos de organização que se confundem Muitas vezes, o problema não é a “organização criminosa” em si, mas a mistura de categorias . Conheça as seguintes famílias: Organizações criminosas (OC) – estruturas cuja finalidade é o lucro ilícito (tráfico, evasão fiscal, corrupção estruturada). Podem ter hierarquia, mas não são Estados nem forças armadas. Redes de apoio / comércio informal – redes que existem para partilha de recursos, proteção mútua ou subsistência, mas que podem ser instrumentalizadas por OC. Grupos de resistência política / civis armados – podem ser legítimos ou ilegítimos consoante o enquadramento legal do Estado. A distinção é jurídica, e não apenas moral. Forças de segurança do Estado – polícia, militares, serviços de inteligência. Têm mandato, formação e (em tese) responsabilidade perante a lei. Glossário rápido Inocente : não apresenta elementos objetivos de participação num crime. Criminoso : pessoa contra a qual existe prova (ou elementos de prova) suficiente para sustentar uma acusação. Suspeito : pessoa sobre a qual recaem indícios, mas sem padrão conclusivo. A distinção é técnica, não emocional. 1.2 Crime é crime — quem quer que o cometa Uma decisão errada é grave onde e quando for cometida . Se uma força de segurança atua com exagero, desrespeita inocentes ou recolhe provas de forma ilícita, a responsabilidade é da entidade que atua , e não de “ter mau comportamento porque o outro também é mau”. Exemplo de raciocínio incorreto (a evitar): Erro no raciocínio “Se a organização criminosa já recorreu à violência, a polícia também pode exagerar.” Isto é uma dupla medida : substitui a lei pela retaliação. A força de Estado perde legitimidade quando copia a desonestidade alheia. 1.3 Porque razão a diferenciação é uma técnica, e não uma opinião Diferenciar o inocente do criminoso exige padrões observáveis e prova , e não impressões. O raciocínio base utiliza: comportamento cognoscível (e não opiniões); traços de comunicação (canal, ritmo, linguagem, repetição); indicadores económicos (fluxo de recursos, armadilhas financeiras, contas falsas); relacionamentos documentados (quem está sempre no centro, quem é periférico); atuação narrativa (quem decide, quem apenas obedece). A: grupo legítimo / de apoio · B: organização criminosa · ⬤ centro operacional Grupo legítimo Organização criminosa Interface de contacto Dinâmica: estruturas fluidas, não estáticas 1.4 Sobre o que se sabe: fontes de informação legítimas Para conhecermos a atividade de uma OC sem nos tornarmos numa OC, recorremos a fontes e métodos que preservam a legalidade: observação pública e aberta (presença, padrões de movimento, fachada comercial falsa); inteligência de fontes abertas (OSINT): registos comerciais, comunicação pública, publicações, grupos de referência, anomalias nas comunicações; inteligência humana (HUMINT) através de fontes próprias, cuja identidade e segurança são devidamente protegidas; análise de comunicações com respeito pelo enquadramento legal e pelas limitações de intervenção livre; análise económica e financeira: rastreio de fluxos, titularidade de empresas, movimentos anómalos. Nível 1 concluído? Compreenda a diferença de abordagem no Nível 2 . Avançar → Nível 2 Nota: este manual tem carácter educativo e não substitui a instrução jurídica, operacional ou ética interna. As referências indicadas são materiais de apoio; em cada contexto, consulte o ordenamento jurídico aplicável. Nível 2 Ler a estrutura: como identificar atividade, influência e comando Mesmo sem atuar diretamente como militar ou polícia, é possível aprender a ler uma rede a partir de sinais , padrões e repetições . Este nível ensina a leitura técnica de redes e grupos. 2.1 As redes não são árvores Muitas organizações criminosas parecem hierárquicas, mas na prática funcionam como redes compostas por: nós centrais (poucos, com muita influência); nós periféricos (muitos, com pouca influência); pontes de contacto (nós que ligam dois subgrupos); rotas de comunicação (canal principal, canais de reserva); e lacunas (espaços onde a informação não passa — úteis para isolamento). 2.2 O que se observa Frequência de comunicação — quem aparece sempre, quem desaparece e reaparece, quem nunca aparece; Assinatura de canal — canal de comunicação preferido, padrão repetido, fuso horário/horário de atividade, marcas linguísticas (forma de expressão); Movimento de pessoas — quem se desloca constantemente, quem permanece fixo, quem apenas surge em condições específicas; Foco de decisão — a operação segue sempre a mesma pessoa ou coligação? Quem corrige, quem desvia. Nó central (centro de comando/influência) Nós ligados Nós periféricos Leitura: ligações mais sólidas = relações mais estáveis 2.3 Como desenvolver uma análise rigorosa recolher dados sem preconceitos — começar com padrões e não com suposições; notar anomalias relacionais, e não apenas “pessoas que parecem suspeitas”; fazer a distinção entre correlação e causalidade — “aparecerem juntos” não prova cumplicidade; “decidirem e agirem em conjunto” já pesa mais; cruzar fontes: se a comunicação aponta para um centro, mas a atividade económica aponta para outro, há uma camada a descobrir. Técnica de leitura “Quando o comandante não é visível, observe quem corrige o rumo quando a operação falha. O verdadeiro centro costuma revelar-se nos momentos de tensão, e não nos momentos de rotina.” 2.4 Inserção / acesso sem recurso à “força” Para entrar num grupo sem revelar a identidade de força de segurança, a estratégia base consiste na adoção de um papel : não surgir como um observador externo, mas sim como alguém com interesses convergentes (não necessariamente criminais — por exemplo, alguém com dúvidas ou alguém que “julga poder ajudar”); parâmetros de comunicação compatíveis (canal, linguagem, ritmo, paciência); evitar forçar a posição; a infiltração resulta melhor quando o grupo sente que o contacto é desinteressado ou útil. Grupo-alvo Observador / agente com papel próximo Aproximação sem revelar a origem — observação prévia ao envolvimento Nível 2 concluído? Vamos confrontar a teoria com exemplos reais no Nível 3. Avançar → Nível 3 Nível 3 Abordagens psicológicas e sociais: compreensão, influência e decisões corretas As competências que melhoram a análise não são estritamente técnicas — são também psicológicas e sociais . Este nível explora como a leitura de pessoas e grupos previne decisões erradas. 3.1 Leitura psicológica de grupos Os grupos (criminosos ou não) partilham dinâmicas semelhantes: Inércia grupal — o grupo tende a manter a direção uma vez estabelecida, mesmo quando o contexto muda; Liderança informal — nem sempre o líder é quem formalmente comanda; muitas vezes é quem corrige, quem medeia conflitos ou quem mantém a rede unida; A comunicação não-verbal é fundamental — o silêncio, o ritmo, quem fala menos e quem fala mais revelam frequentemente mais do que aquilo que é verbalizado; Vulnerabilidade social — os grupos são frágeis nas suas dependências estruturais: comunicação, recursos, confiança e acesso a pessoas-chave. 3.2 Influência sem coerção É possível influenciar um grupo sem recorrer à força, à detenção ou à violência direta: alterar as perceções de risco (sem recorrer a mentiras — através da disponibilidade de informação, do exemplo ou de alterações contextuais); alterar os incentivos (por exemplo, tornando mais oneroso o uso de uma determinada rede do que de outra); isolar lentamente os pontos centrais — não por destruição direta, mas através do desgaste de confiança; compreender que o grupo responde a normas internas — caso essas normas se tornem contraditórias, o grupo tende a desestabilizar-se. Atenção A influência não visa a manipulação para fins criminosos. Constitui um instrumento de análise: utilizar a perceção e a dinâmica para compreender o funcionamento do grupo e avaliar quando é possível desmantelá-lo sem derramamento de sangue ou detenções indevidas. 3.3 Quando não é necessário deter nem abater Muitas vezes, o problema reside em apenas uma parte da rede , e não na rede na sua totalidade. A decisão mais precisa é aquela que: visa diretamente a pessoa ou atividade verdadeiramente responsável; evita a punição genérica e indiscriminada; protege os inocentes que orbitam em redor do grupo; preserva a legitimidade da força de segurança. As detenções ou o recurso à força devem ser proporcionais e fundamentados em provas , e nunca motivados pela dimensão da rede, pela impaciência ou pelo espírito de vingança. 3.4 Riscos de uma análise incorreta tomar o comportamento por prova — o facto de alguém estar “sempre junto” não constitui prova de culpa; análise por perfil — discriminar com base na aparência, origem ou associação revela incompetência técnica e injustiça legal; viés de confirmação — partir do pressuposto de que “aquele grupo é totalmente corrupto” cega o investigador para identificar quem é inocente no seu interior. 3.5 Quem sabe o que sabe — e porque razão isso importa Para conhecer a atividade de um grupo, é necessário dispor de fontes externas ao grupo e observá-lo de dentro para fora . Isto implica: observar o que é público, mas sabendo ler nas entrelinhas; ouvir o que a própria comunidade diz sobre o grupo (sem ecoar meros rumores); compreender que a “intelligence” (informação) não se resume à espionagem — é também a perceção de padrões sociais repetidos; evitar confundir o relato das fontes com a verdade absoluta — toda a informação deve ser verificada, cruzada e ponderada. Referências externas para aprofundamento (Nível 3) UNODC — Gabinete das Nações Unidas contra a Droga e o Crime — materiais sobre estruturas criminosas transnacionais e respostas do Estado. INTERPOL — Recursos sobre criminalidade organizada e cooperação internacional . ICAO — Normas e padrões de cooperação em investigações internacionais (contexto de apoio técnico). Materiais de análise de redes (teoria de grafos aplicada à análise de relações) e de inteligência de fontes abertas (OSINT) — consulte orientações nacionais e internacionais sobre o uso ético. Agora que leu os três níveis, veja um exemplo concreto de como as abordagens diferem. Ir ao Exemplo Real Exemplo Real Polícia e Militares: como as abordagens diferem entre países — e porque razão a distinção recai sempre sobre o crime e a inocência Não existe uma “polícia portuguesa vs. militar francesa vs. polícia italiana” como modelos mutuamente exclusivos. Existe uma variedade de modelos nacionais , cada um com os seus limites, formas e normas. Contudo, o princípio é transversal: o crime é crime, o inocente é inocente — onde quer que ocorram. 4.1 Tipos de modelos de forças de segurança (visão panorâmica) Polícia civil unificada — modelo em que a polícia constitui a principal força de segurança no domínio civil, com funções de investigação, prevenção e resposta, podendo contemplar detalhes por tipo de crime (por exemplo, polícia judiciária, forças especiais). Forças armadas com papel interno — em determinados países, as forças armadas podem desempenhar um papel na segurança interna em situações específicas (estado de sítio, operações de apoio, segurança de infraestruturas críticas). A presença militar interna deve ser excecional e estritamente regulada. Modelos com forças especializadas — alguns países organizam forças consoante o tipo de ameaça (unidades de resposta rápida, unidades de investigação criminal, unidades de inteligência). A especialização tem valor quando existem competências distintas, mas não deve substituir a coordenação legal. Coordenação internacional — muitas ameaças são transnacionais, pelo que a resposta ocorre frequentemente através de cooperação (INTERPOL, Europol, acordos bilaterais, partilha de inteligência). 4.2 O que muda entre países (e o que permanece igual) Dimensão O que varia O que não varia Enquadramento legal de cada força Estatutos, competências, limites de uso da força, procedimentos de detenção. Nenhuma força de Estado pode ignorar o princípio de que atos criminosos cometidos por agentes constituem crimes. Relação entre militares e civis Cada país define quando e de que forma as forças armadas podem intervir internamente. A distinção entre inocente e criminoso não desaparece pela presença de tropas nas ruas. Estrutura de investigação Nível de especialização, coordenação entre serviços, papel da inteligência. A prova e o devido processo legal são obrigatórios em qualquer sistema que pretenda ser justo. Cooperação internacional Grau de integração em redes regionais e globais. A criminalidade organizada não respeita fronteiras — a resposta não pode cingir-se ao plano puramente nacional. 4.3 A diferença real entre polícias — um exemplo concreto Consideremos uma situação hipotética (mas estruturalmente comum): uma organização criminosa que opera através de redes de comércio fictícias , com comunicação encriptada e presença em múltiplas jurisdições. Abordagem puramente repressiva (modelo rígido) : operação simultânea em múltiplos pontos, detenções genéricas, apreensões massivas. Vantagem: impacto rápido. Risco: detenção de pessoas sem ligação relevante; provas frágeis; desconfiança da comunidade; reação de adaptação rápida por parte do grupo. Abordagem de inteligência e análise (modelo de leitura) : mapeamento da estrutura, identificação de centros e pontes, distinção entre elementos centrais e periféricos, atuação sobre indicadores específicos. Vantagem: precisão, menor risco de erro face a inocentes, preservação da legitimidade. Requer tempo, coordenação e rigor. Ambas podem ser necessárias em momentos distintos. O erro ocorre quando se utiliza apenas uma por impulso, ou quando a via repressiva é usada para substituir a análise. 4.4 A mesma falha em qualquer contexto Se uma polícia portuguesa comete um excesso, constitui um erro português. Se uma força militar italiana excede a autorização interna, constitui um erro italiano. Se uma polícia francesa desrespeita um inocente, constitui um erro francês. Se um elemento policial ou militar de qualquer país comete um crime, o crime é crime . Um ato criminoso não se torna “menos crime” por ser praticado por um Estado ou instituição. Princípio O Estado que atua com as mãos sujas perde a autoridade moral para agir — mesmo que o outro lado seja criminoso. Por seu turno, o criminoso não se torna “menos criminoso” pelo facto de a polícia ter agido incorretamente. Dois erros não melhoram o mundo; tornam ambos os lados ilegítimos. 4.5 Resposta correta: precisão e não exagero coordenar a atuação entre jurisdições quando a rede é transnacional; distinguir os membros efetivos da estrutura criminosa daqueles que são periféricos, inocentes ou meramente relacionados por proximidade; agir com base em provas, e não em pressões mediáticas ou reputacionais; manter a transparência interna e externa no tocante às decisões — porque demonstrar que a força atua dentro de limites é o que garante a sua legitimidade. Agora que leu a teoria e o exemplo, valide os seus conhecimentos. Ir ao Quiz Quiz de validação — recomendado após a leitura dos níveis Responda a cada questão. No final, clique em “Enviar respostas” para verificar o seu resultado. 1. Qual é a diferença fundamental entre “inocente” e “criminoso” num contexto técnico? A) Quem está sempre no centro do grupo é automaticamente criminoso. B) Depende de elementos de prova e padrões observáveis, e não de impressões ou da posição no grupo. C) Quem nunca se desloca é considerado inocente. 2. Um investigador pensa: “A organização criminosa já foi violenta, logo a polícia também pode exagerar.” Esta constitui uma boa decisão? A) Sim, porque o crime justifica o crime. B) Não, trata-se de uma dupla medida — substitui a lei pela retaliação e compromete a legitimidade do Estado. C) Depende do país em questão. 3. Na leitura de redes criminosas, quem é frequentemente o verdadeiro centro de comando? A) Quem aparece mais vezes na comunicação pública. B) A pessoa que corrige o rumo quando a operação falha, mesmo que não seja a mais visível. C) Quem nunca aparece. 4. Relativamente a uma rede criminosa, é sempre necessário efetuar detenções ou usar a força pelo simples facto de a rede existir? A) Sim, porque a existência da rede constitui prova de crime contra todos os membros. B) Não — muitas vezes o problema afeta apenas uma parte da rede; a decisão deve ser precisa, proporcional e fundamentada em provas. C) Apenas se houver pressão política. 5. Um crime cometido por um agente de polícia ou militar constitui: A) Um ato menos grave, pois o agente atua no interesse do Estado. B) Um crime — idêntico na sua natureza a qualquer outro; a origem institucional não diminui a ilegalidade. C) Uma conduta aceitável se o grupo-alvo também for criminoso. 6. Para conhecer a atividade de um grupo sem assumir o papel de força repressiva direta, pode recorrer-se a: A) Exclusivamente a espionagem não regulada. B) Observação pública, inteligência de fontes abertas (OSINT), HUMINT através de fontes próprias e análise de padrões, dentro do enquadramento legal. C) Não é possível obter qualquer conhecimento sem pertencer ao grupo. 7. A diferença entre os modelos policiais e militares de diferentes países traduz-se, em última análise, em: A) Aspetos puramente cosméticos — o crime é igual em todo o lado, e o princípio da inocência/culpa é transversal. B) A legislação define competências e limites, mas o princípio de que o crime é crime e o inocente é inocente não varia com a nacionalidade. C) Não existem diferenças — todos os países aplicam exatamente os mesmos métodos. Nentoo: What "we" Know Gentoo Linux is a Source Based distribution that ask users to compile all software. While it gives a sensation of control, software compatibility is very restricted and their repositories have a lot of software that is out of date and incompatible to install on Gentoo, without facing more problems on compilation time. The Unique aspect of control that can give, it to those users who know the work of LFS aka Linux From Scratch , and want that process automated, while LFS don't face so much problems installing software. After that, Gentoo offer the possibility to manage compatibility in Software, using the USE flags, that are "words" defined on the software, pointing into the compatibility. For example, Vim on Gentoo , can be installed without the Graphical interface, by adding something like this: app-editors/vim -X . With that value placed in the correct path /etc/portage/package.use/ , as a content of the filename of the software(vim), Gentoo knows that Vim , will not have Graphical compatibility. It simplifies the process of installing software without personalizing it with the core options that the authors give. In fact, all that painful process of extracting to / or other path each library and applications, ./configure --help Options, that can be More deeper than what Gentoo gives to users, and the make & make install to install software, can have extra options too. Since Gentoo wish to simplify that process, Gentoo serve that purpose only . A interesting aspect between Gentoo and FreeBSD , is that Gentoo change the magic words of software compatibility when compiling, while FreeBSD don't care what "software compatibility" you want, when compiling software from ports . The "reconfig" option when compiling software using FreeBSD ports, is the best option to save you time. Else, you will need to Monitor compilation process, waiting for a new "popup" about software compatibility, of each extra software that some software ask as dependency. In the other hand/side, Debian already compile everything and offer the same, almost all other Linux Distros offer: Binary Packages (already compiled software). Click any wall to open its internals, code and sources. 🛡 pledge(2) — voluntary amputation of power + What: a process declares which syscall groups it needs — e.g. stdio rpath wpath cpath inet dns — and the kernel kills it ( SIGABRT ) if it ever touches anything else. Promises can only shrink, never grow. A compromised httpd parser that pledged stdio rpath cannot exec , open sockets, or ptrace — the exploit dies inside the sandbox it built itself. copy /* httpd render path: after parsing config, drop everything */ #include <unistd.h> if (pledge( "stdio rpath" , NULL) == -1) err(1, "pledge" ); /* from here: no exec, no socket, no prot_exec — RCE becomes DoS */ Why secure: moves policy into the program where intent is known; tiny API (one call) so adoption is massive — 500+ base programs pledged. Combines with unveil for least privilege in two dimensions. Sources: pledge(2) manual · innovations · sshd + privsep 👁 unveil(2) — the filesystem you can't see doesn't exist + What: grant visibility to only chosen paths with chosen rights ( rwxc ), then lock: unveil("/var/www","r"); unveil(NULL,NULL) . Everything else returns ENOENT — directory traversal, /etc/passwd reads, key theft all fail closed. Perfect pair: pledge limits what calls , unveil limits what files . copy /* static file server: see only /var/www, read-only */ unveil( "/var/www" , "r" ); unveil( "/var/www/logs" , "rwc" ); if (pledge( "stdio rpath wpath cpath" , NULL) == -1) err(1, "pledge" ); unveil(NULL, NULL); // lock: no more unveil calls Sources: unveil(2) · innovations ✖ W^X — memory is writable XOR executable, never both + What: since 3.3, strict by default in 6.0: no page may be WRITE+EXEC . RedTeams: Home Red / Teams Adversary emulation · doctrine, lab, tooling Red Teams: emulating an adversary, not running a scanner A red team is measured by the objective it reaches and the evidence it leaves behind, not by the number of alerts it generates. This page is the working half of that idea: how engagements are scoped, which documents define the tradecraft, how to build a lab you can burn without burning a client, and which tools answer which question at each phase. authorised targets only 12 tool groups 5 lab components 6 doctrines 01 Red team, pentest, scan The words are used interchangeably in sales decks and that is where most disappointment begins. A vulnerability scan enumerates; a penetration test proves a finding on an agreed asset list; a red team is given an objective — a specific data store, a domain admin, a production change — and is judged on whether it gets there without being detected for an agreed period. Engagement Question answered Success looks like Typical shape Vulnerability assessment What is out of date or misconfigured? A prioritised list with evidence Days, tool-driven, broad Penetration test Can these specific findings be exploited? Proof per finding, with remediation One to three weeks, asset list Red team Can a realistic adversary reach the objective? Objective reached, detection timeline reported Weeks, stealth-weighted, few targets Adversary emulation Do our detections catch this known actor? Coverage map of techniques, not a breach Days, TTP-driven, instrumented Emulation is the strictest and most useful of the four: you pick a threat actor that actually targets your sector, replay its techniques in order, and measure what the defenders saw. The difference between "we got domain admin" and "we got domain admin in 40 minutes and nobody noticed" is the whole deliverable. 02 Scope and rules of engagement Everything below assumes a signed scope, a named deconfliction contact and a stop condition. Without those three, the same commands are a criminal offence — capability is not permission. The manual covers the legal baseline in detail; here is the operational version used to build a red team RoE. RoE field What it must say Why red teams get it wrong Objective The exact asset, account or outcome that counts as success "Get in somehow" produces an unfalsifiable report Targets Domains, IPs, tenants, offices, people in scope — plus exclusions Third-party SaaS and cloud regions silently enter scope Techniques Allowed, discouraged and forbidden actions, by name Nobody wrote down "no social engineering" Deconfliction Who knows, how they are reached, how a test is proved genuine The blue team escalates a real incident mid-engagement Stop Conditions that end the test immediately, and who may call them Outages and safety incidents have no agreed brake Data What may be taken, where it lives, when it is destroyed Client records end up in a screenshot folder Write the get-out-of-jail letter before the first packet The authorisation should name the testers, the dates, the assets, the permitted techniques and a contact who can confirm the engagement at any hour. If an operator is stopped by a system owner at two in the morning, that document is the difference between an incident and a phone call. Keep it offline as well as on the phone. 03 The documents that define the work Red teaming has a literature. Reading it once turns improvisation into a repeatable method, and it is what separates a report a client can act on from a wall of screenshots. Document Publisher What you take from it ATT&CK MITRE The tactic and technique vocabulary every finding is mapped to Adversary Emulation Library MITRE Engenuity Ready-made emulation plans per threat group TIBER-EU European Central Bank Threat-intelligence-led red teaming for financial entities CBEST Bank of England The same idea with UK supervisory reporting hooks PTES PTES project The phase structure a report is expected to follow SP 800-115 NIST Method for penetration testing and assessment, with evidence guidance For the defensive half of the same vocabulary, see lab . ATT&CK is also the bridge to APT reporting: an actor profile without technique IDs is folklore, and a technique without telemetry is untestable. 04 Build an attack lab Rehearse on systems that cannot call a lawyer. The lab below is deliberately small: one hypervisor, three isolated networks, a Windows domain to attack, a Linux host to pivot through, and a C2 server that only the lab can reach. Everything is snapshotted, because a lab you cannot roll back teaches the wrong lesson about persistence. Layer Build Purpose Reset Hypervisor Proxmox VE, or VirtualBox/VMware on a dedicated host Snapshots, cloning, network isolation Weekly rebuild Attack net 10.66.0.0/24, no NAT route to the internet Kali, C2, redirector VM Revert C2 after each drill Target net 10.66.10.0/24, firewall between the two DC, workstations, Linux server, vulnerable apps Snapshot per exercise Domain Windows Server DC plus two Windows clients, weak-but-realistic policy Kerberos, SMB, GPO, tiered admin mistakes Rebuild via Ansible/GOAD Targets DVWA, Juice Shop, Metasploitable, an old AP you own Web, network and wireless practice Container recreate # one isolated bridge, no NAT: the lab cannot reach the internet by accident sudo ip link add br-red type bridge sudo ip addr add 10.66.0.1/24 dev br-red sudo ip link set br-red up # a web target you are allowed to break docker network create --subnet 10.66.10.0/24 redlab docker run -d --name juice --net redlab --ip 10.66.10.50 \ -p 10.66.10.50:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop # snapshot the domain controller before every exercise virsh snapshot-create-as dc01 baseline-$(date +%F) --description "clean AD" # and a resolver that cannot leak your real queries sudo systemd-resolve --interface br-red --set-dns 10.66.10.10 Lab rules that keep it honest No lab traffic to the internet. One NAT rule and your test domain starts appearing in outside logs. Snapshot before every drill and revert after it. Persistence in the lab is how you learn to clean up. Write the command log as you go: script -a lab/$(date +%F).log turns a session into evidence. Break the lab on purpose. Restore a domain, corrupt a policy, then fix it — that is the incident you will meet later. Keep a second lab for detections. The defenders need the same topology with sensors attached. 05 Walkthrough: from nothing to hacking The table above is the plan; this is the build. Work through it in order, because a lab that fails at step two turns every later result into a guess. Every command assumes a Debian host with virtualisation and a lab that cannot reach the internet. 0. Starting from nothing Before a hypervisor there is a laptop, a terminal and a lot of theory. The order that works: Linux and the shell, then how packets actually move, then a scripting language so the tooling repeats itself, then this lab. A week per stage is enough if you finish the exercises instead of reading them. Linux and the shell. Files, permissions, services, logs, and enough Bash to loop over a target list without copying commands by hand. Networking. TCP and UDP packets , DNS , HTTP , and the rest of the networking manual. Coding. Python to parse scan output and call APIs, curl for the raw request, and the cli habit of building one small tool per repetitive task. Containers. The Docker manual, because half the targets in this lab are one container away. 1. Host and hypervisor sudo apt install -y qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-system virtinst libosinfo-bin sudo usermod -aG libvirt,kvm "$USER" # log out and back in virt-host-validate # the KVM answers must be OK 2. Two isolated networks, no NAT cat > /tmp/red-attack.xml <<'XML' <network> <name>red-attack</name> <bridge name="virbr-reda"/> <ip address="10.66.0.1" netmask="255.255.255.0"> <dhcp><range start="10.66.0.100" end="10.66.0.150"/></dhcp> </ip> </network> XML virsh net-define /tmp/red-attack.xml virsh net-start red-attack && virsh net-autostart red-attack virsh net-list --all Repeat for red-target on 10.66.10.0/24 .
